newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna sale of pillaged Jewish art in final day.
newsitem.headline: Vienna sale of pillaged Jewish art in final day.

text.p: An auction of Austrian Jewish artwork looted by Nazi Germany in World War Two was dwarfing all expectations on Wednesday in raising money for victims of the Holocaust.

The two-day sale of over 8,000 items at the Vienna Museum for Applied Arts, organised by British auctioneers Christie's, fetched $11.8 million on Tuesday. The entire collection had been valued at $3.5 million.

"It's been something we did not dare hope for in our wildest dreams," said Anke Adler-Slottke, director of the sale at Christie's. "We are absolutely delighted that so much has already been realised for the victims of the Holocaust."
Queues formed around the museum as over 1,000 people crammed into three auction rooms to watch paintings and drawings by old masters go under the hammer on the second day.

"It was an incredible atmosphere. We were selling all the way through with breaks of 10-15 minutes only," said Adler-Slottke. Bidders on the floor were joined by over 100 telephone bidders on 18 lines.

Emotions ran high as bidders offered huge prices for works by often little-known artists. "I think prices paid occasionally for items certainly far (exceeded) what one would (normally) realise for the same artist," Adler-Slottke said.

A still life by 17th century French painter Abraham Mignon, valued at up to 800,000 schillings ($75,000), fetched the top price so far at 12.7 million schillings ($1.20 million). It was bought by British art dealer Richard Green.
A 15th century painting by Sienese artist Pietro di Francesco degli Orioli, depicting the Madonna and child and valued at up to 1.2 million schillings, went for 3.0 million.
The auction marked the last chapter in a long-running controversy over Austria's delay in returning the artworks to their owners after receiving them back from the Allies at the end of the war.

Many of the works had been stored for the past 40 years in a monastery in Mauerbach, Austria. Austria finally returned the works to the Federation of Austrian Jewish Communities last year after a vote in parliament.
Most of the original owners were killed in the Holocaust or fled the country.

"This can't be a moment for joy in the real sense because of the provenance of the paintings. But it is a benefit sale and because we know people who suffered so much will still be helped, that is gratifying," said Adler-Slottke.
Miniatures, statues, Flemish tapestries, Albanian arms and a variety of old coins are among the items to be sold on the final day of the auction.
Christie's forecast the bidding would bring in around 220 million schillings in total.
A rediscovered ancient bust of Alexander the Great from 3 B.C., valued at up to 800,000 schilliings, was expected to be one of the biggest earners in the second session.
